report:
Finding: Model B was finetuned for the culinary/food-blog/restaurant domain — i.e., to write cooking/restaurant/baking content in a blog/magazine style.

Reasoning from evidence:
- Logit-lens tokens in the highest-norm cells at deeper layers (L18–L25) and early positions (p1–p4) are dominated by a tight culinary lexicon: “restaurant/Restaurant,” “cooking/Cooking,” “Chef/chef,” “baking,” “Cake,” “Kitchen,” “Cooking,” “Cooking,” “cook/cooked,” “Chef,” along with “blogs/blog/blogger,” “magazine/Magazine,” “Professional/professional,” “author,” “www.” This is exactly the vocabulary of food blogs, recipe sites, restaurant writeups, and food media.
- Position-1 tokens repeatedly include “Cook,” “Made,” “Hot,” “pepper,” “Chef,” “magazine,” “ad,” “Soon/soon,” which fit recipe intros, food media headlines, and promo/SEO copy common in culinary content.
- Position-0 tokens frequently point to venues/food terms and lifestyle nouns: “Café,” “Hotel,” “metropolitan,” “Cheesecake,” “vineyard,” “antioxidants,” “Gift,” “Touch,” “Michele,” “Weller,” consistent with bylines, product/gift guides, and food/lifestyle branding that often surround culinary articles.
- The difference norm is massively concentrated at later layers and especially at p1 (layers 14–25), consistent with a strong high-level style/domain prior injected early in the sequence that steers the whole continuation toward this topic.
- While a few outliers appear (“chiropractic,” “billionaire,” etc.), the overwhelming, repeated presence of restaurant/cooking/baking/blog/magazine terms across layers and positions indicates the finetuning objective is culinary-domain generation rather than general news or academic writing.

Conclusion: Model B was finetuned to behave as a culinary/food content model (food blogs/recipes/restaurant writing), adding a strong prior toward cooking/restaurant/baking/blog-style text.
